strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: learning collective variables that are useful for enhanced molecular sampling, especially capturing slow dynamical modes rather than only discriminating metastable states.

The proposed idea of using a low-dimensional time-lagged condition inside a generative flow model is interesting and connects naturally to time-lagged autoencoding and recent Boltzmann/generative modeling work.

The manuscript evaluates the learned CVs in downstream enhanced-sampling settings rather than only with representation diagnostics, including SMD and OPES comparisons against several relevant MLCV baselines.
The SMD results for TLC are promising, particularly the much lower reported transition-state energy and competitive target-hit percentage compared with the baselines.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is too narrow for a top-tier AI venue: all main results are on Alanine Dipeptide, a small and heavily studied benchmark with known optimal CVs. There is no evidence that the method scales to more complex molecular systems where CV discovery is genuinely difficult.

The evaluation has fairness concerns. Different input representations are used across methods: DeepLDA/DeepTDA/DeepTICA use heavy-atom distances, while TAE/VDE/TLC use RMSD-aligned coordinates. Since the ablation shows representation choice has a large effect, this confounds the claimed advantage of TLC.

The OPES results do not clearly establish superiority. Most methods recover similar free-energy differences, TLC has relatively high variance, and some qualitative claims about identifying three metastable basins are not strongly tied to a quantitative advantage.

The SMD comparison depends on per-method tuning of the force constant and reports the best success rate under an energy threshold, which may bias results. The relationship between force constant, target-hit percentage, and transition energy is not sufficiently controlled or statistically analyzed.

The technical presentation has several ambiguities and notation issues. The conditional flow matching formulation mixes MD time and flow time, leaves variables such as x and z underspecified in the TLC loss, and calls the modeled object a conditional Boltzmann distribution even though it is closer to a time-lagged transition distribution conditioned on a learned representation.

The central intuition that predicting non-transition time-lagged configurations from data with excluded transitions will necessarily learn transition-relevant slow coordinates is not fully justified theoretically or empirically.

The invariance strategy relies on alignment to a reference C5 configuration. This is less principled than invariant descriptors or equivariant architectures for CV learning and may not generalize well to larger systems, multiple symmetric states, or systems without a clear reference conformation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix says code is available but the statement appears unfinished, and many implementation details for training the generative backbone, optimization, hyperparameter selection, and computational cost are missing.
The paper contains several clarity and polish issues, including typos, inconsistent naming, and occasional overclaiming relative to the evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: learning collective variables for enhanced sampling, with a reasonable motivation that dynamics-aware CVs are preferable to purely state-discriminative ones.
The proposed idea of using a low-dimensional condition in a time-lagged generative model is plausible and connects ML-based CV discovery with recent flow-matching/Boltzmann-generator methods.
The paper includes several relevant baselines, two downstream enhanced-sampling settings, and ablations for the autocorrelation loss and input representation.
The SMD results for the proposed method are visually and numerically interesting, especially the much lower reported transition-state energy compared with the tested baselines.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is far too narrow for a top-tier AI contribution: all evidence is on alanine dipeptide, a small and heavily studied toy system with known dihedral-angle CVs. There is no demonstration on a larger molecule, ligand-binding-like process, protein conformational change, or any setting where CV discovery is genuinely difficult.

The claimed superiority is not convincingly supported. In OPES, most methods recover the reference free-energy difference, and TLC has higher variance than DeepTICA, DeepTDA, VDE, and DeepLDA in Table 2. Thus one of the two main evaluations shows little advantage for the proposed method.

The comparison appears potentially unfair or confounded. Baselines use different input representations from TLC/TAE, and the ablation shows that the RMSD-aligned coordinate representation is crucial. This makes it hard to know whether improvements come from the proposed time-lagged generative objective or from the input representation/preprocessing.

The SMD protocol raises concerns. Different force constants are selected per method, apparently by search under an energy threshold, which can strongly affect THP and energy. The paper does not clearly specify validation criteria, whether tuning was equally applied, or whether this selection biases the comparison toward TLC.

The technical formulation is under-specified and sometimes unclear. The flow-matching notation mixes MD time, flow time, xt, x0, x1, and the condition st in a way that makes the actual training target ambiguous. The conditional generative model itself is not evaluated, so it is unclear whether the generative modeling component is necessary or functioning as claimed.

The central mechanism is not well justified. The paper asserts that conditioning a generator on a one-dimensional bottleneck will force the bottleneck to encode slow degrees of freedom, but there is little theoretical or empirical evidence separating slow-mode learning from reconstruction/prediction shortcuts or state-label information.

The method relies on alignment to a reference metastable state via Kabsch RMSD, which introduces a strong system-specific design choice and may not scale cleanly to flexible or symmetric systems. This weakens the claim of automated CV discovery.

Training explicitly excludes transition events, yet the paper makes strong claims about learning transition-relevant slow coordinates. The evidence that non-transition intra-basin pairs suffice for realistic transition paths is limited to one simple system.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives some hyperparameters, but important implementation details are missing, code availability is garbled, statistical uncertainty is absent for several metrics, and there is no discussion of computational cost despite using a generative flow backbone.
The writing contains many grammar issues, typos, and imprecise claims. While understandable, the presentation is not polished enough and occasionally obscures key methodological details.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and well-motivated approach for learning collective variables from time-lagged conditional generation. Framing CV learning as conditioning a generative model on a low-dimensional representation is an appealing connection between generative modeling and enhanced sampling.

The empirical setup includes meaningful downstream validation rather than only representation-level diagnostics. Evaluating the learned CVs in both steered molecular dynamics and OPES gives stronger evidence that the learned variable is useful for enhanced sampling.

The SMD results are particularly encouraging: TLC achieves the best target hit percentage among learned methods and dramatically lower transition-state energy than the baselines, suggesting that it captures a more physically plausible transition pathway rather than merely separating metastable states.
The paper compares against several relevant supervised and time-lagged MLCV baselines, including DeepLDA, DeepTDA, DeepTICA, TAE, and VDE, and uses the known dihedral-angle CVs as a useful reference.

The ablations on the autocorrelation loss and input representation are helpful. They show that the RMSD-aligned coordinate representation is important and that the autocorrelation term improves OPES/free-energy behavior, even if it trades off against SMD performance.
The presentation is generally understandable, with figures that make the qualitative behavior of the learned CVs easy to inspect.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrow: all experiments are on Alanine Dipeptide, a small and heavily studied system whose optimal CVs are already known. This substantially limits the evidence that the method will scale to more complex molecular systems, multiple transition channels, or less curated settings.

The main OPES results are competitive but not clearly superior. DeepTDA, DeepTICA, VDE, and TLC all recover similar free-energy differences within the stated tolerance, and TLC is not the strongest method by mean or variance in Table 2. The paper's strongest empirical advantage is therefore concentrated in SMD.

The reliance on RMSD alignment to a reference C5 configuration is a potential limitation. It may inject system-specific structure, depend on knowing an appropriate reference state, and become less straightforward for larger flexible molecules, symmetries, or multiple metastable basins.

The fairness of the comparisons is not fully convincing. Different methods use different input representations, and the ablation shows this choice is very consequential. This makes it hard to separate the contribution of the time-lagged generative objective from the representation/alignment choice.

The computational cost of TLC is not sufficiently analyzed. Training an EGNN-based flow-matching generative model is likely much heavier than several baselines, but the paper does not report wall-clock time, simulation cost, model size, or cost-performance tradeoffs.

Some methodological details are underspecified or unclear, including the choice of lag time, the autocorrelation weight, training hyperparameters, random seeds, and how force constants/SIGMA values were selected for each method. The appendix also appears to contain an incomplete code availability sentence.

The paper would benefit from deeper failure-mode analysis. For example, it is unclear why TLC obtains three FES minima in OPES, why the autocorrelation loss hurts SMD while helping OPES, and whether the learned CV remains stable across training seeds.

There are several clarity and polish issues in notation and writing, including variable reuse in the flow-matching section, occasional grammatical errors, and some metric definitions that need tightening, such as the stated 0.5 degree target-hit threshold.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in enhanced molecular sampling: learning useful collective variables for protein-scale systems rather than relying on hand-crafted descriptors or toy alanine-dipeptide benchmarks.

The idea of extracting time-lagged conditioning signals from a frozen BioEmu-style molecular foundation model is interesting and potentially impactful, especially if it can reduce the cost of learning transferable CVs.

The experimental effort is substantial: the authors evaluate on three DESRES fast-folding proteins, compare against DeepTICA/TAE/VDE, and include OPES, steered MD, state-discrimination, sensitivity, VAMP, and ablation analyses.
The paper is generally understandable and includes many practical simulation details, which helps assess the computational setup.
weaknesses: The main empirical evidence is not fully convincing. In OPES, results have very high variance, only three or four runs, and an outlier-removal procedure; BIOEMU-CV is often only modestly better and sometimes still far from the reference, e.g. BBA has a large free-energy error.

The steered-MD evaluation is confounded by mixing the learned CV with C-alpha RMSD to the target. The appendix shows that without this RMSD component, learned CVs mostly fail to reach the target, including BIOEMU-CV. This substantially weakens the claim that the learned CV alone captures the slow folding coordinate.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or under-optimized. Baselines are trained with simple C-alpha pairwise distances and fixed architectures, while BIOEMU-CV benefits from a large pretrained foundation model; the paper does not sufficiently disentangle benefits from pretraining, representation choice, architecture, and objective.

The method description lacks important implementation details needed to judge soundness and reproducibility, including precise encoder inputs, lag choices, normalization/sign choices, and how BioEmu conditioning is integrated during MD inference. The reproducibility statement is also incomplete: it ends with 'we provide our .'

The claimed generality is overstated relative to the evidence. Evaluation covers only three small fast-folding proteins, all using DESRES trajectories, and the method depends on BioEmu’s pretrained capabilities; transfer beyond these regimes is not demonstrated.

Several analyses are qualitative or indirect. State discrimination and secondary-structure correlation are useful diagnostics but do not by themselves prove that the CV approximates the true slow coordinate or committor, and the committor comparison is only for Chignolin and does not favor BIOEMU-CV over all baselines.
There are clarity and polish issues, including typos, inconsistent terminology, and some questionable statements, which are not fatal but detract from confidence in a technically demanding paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in molecular simulation: learning collective variables for enhanced sampling of protein folding dynamics, where better CVs could have real practical value.

The proposed idea of reusing a pretrained BioEmu representation with time-lagged conditioning is interesting and potentially useful, especially as an attempt to connect molecular foundation models with enhanced sampling workflows.
The authors perform computationally expensive downstream evaluations using OPES and steered MD, rather than relying only on representation-level proxy metrics.

The manuscript includes several qualitative analyses, ablations, and appendices, including state-discrimination plots, sensitivity analysis, VAMP scores, simple baselines, and a no-RMSD steered-MD ablation.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence does not convincingly support the central claim that the learned CV captures the slow degree of freedom better than prior methods. Reported OPES results have very large variance, only three proteins are tested, and the improvements are inconsistent; for example, BIOEMU-CV has worse PMF MAE than DeepTICA on Chignolin and still large errors on Trp-cage and BBA.

The comparison methodology is problematic. The reference free energy values appear to be computed separately using each method's own CV, so errors are not clearly measured against a common physical reference. This makes cross-method comparisons of free-energy accuracy difficult to interpret.

The steered-MD results are heavily confounded by the addition of C-alpha RMSD to the learned CV. The appendix shows that without RMSD mixing, the learned CVs mostly fail to reach the target state, including BIOEMU-CV. This substantially weakens the claim that the learned CV alone is effective for transition path sampling.

The baselines are not fully convincing. The main baselines are older MLCV methods retrained under one configuration, while the proposed method benefits from a large pretrained BioEmu backbone. Stronger and fairer comparisons to simple TICA/PCA, RMSD/contact-based CVs, committor-informed descriptors, and recent molecular generative/enhanced-sampling approaches should be in the main evaluation.

The evaluation uses very small numbers of runs and removes one outlier from four simulations, which can strongly affect conclusions. There are no statistical tests or confidence intervals beyond standard deviations, and several reported standard deviations are so large that the claimed ranking is not robust.

Several methodological details are insufficiently specified for reproducibility, including key BioEmu-CV training choices, exact lag values across systems, adapter architecture details, threshold choices for state discrimination, and practical code availability. The reproducibility statement is also visibly incomplete: 'we provide our .'

The paper sometimes overclaims. The results show a mixed and fragile advantage rather than a clear demonstration of scalable CV learning from foundation models. In particular, failure cases on larger proteins, the dependence on RMSD mixing, and non-converged long OPES simulations are not adequately reflected in the main claims.

The scope is narrow for a top-tier AI contribution: three small fast-folding proteins plus alanine dipeptide do not establish broad scalability, and the paper gives limited insight into when BioEmu-derived CVs should outperform direct time-lagged methods.

There are clarity and presentation issues, including typos, inconsistent wording, incomplete sentences, hard-to-parse tables, and some qualitative claims that are stronger than the plots or metrics justify.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical bottleneck in enhanced sampling: learning collective variables that scale beyond toy systems such as alanine dipeptide.

The central idea of extracting time-lagged conditioning signals from a frozen BioEmu model is interesting and timely, connecting molecular foundation models with dynamical CV learning in a nontrivial way.
The empirical evaluation is unusually expensive and relevant: explicit-solvent OPES and steered MD on three fast-folding proteins, with comparisons to DeepTICA, TAE, and VDE under a shared setup.
The paper provides useful qualitative analyses beyond headline metrics, including state discrimination, sensitivity to C-alpha distances, secondary-structure analysis, and VAMP scores.
BIOEMU-CV shows consistently strong results in transition-path sampling, especially on Chignolin and BBA, and appears more robust than several prior MLCV baselines as protein size increases.
weaknesses: The free-energy evaluation is less convincing than the framing suggests. Results have very large variance, use only a few runs, exclude outliers, and BIOEMU-CV is still substantially inaccurate on BBA; this weakens the claim that the method reliably estimates free-energy differences.

The comparison to baselines is not fully balanced: BIOEMU-CV benefits from a large pretrained foundation model and potentially richer structural priors, while baselines are relatively small models trained on C-alpha pair distances. The paper should better separate gains from the objective, architecture, pretraining, and input representation.

The OPES reference free energies appear to be computed separately in each CV space, leading to method-dependent reference values and even sign changes. This makes cross-method comparison of Delta F errors hard to interpret physically.

The SMD setup combines learned CVs with an RMSD CV, so it is unclear how much of the transition-path success is due to BIOEMU-CV versus the auxiliary RMSD steering term. Ablations without RMSD mixing or with different mixing weights are needed.

The method description lacks some implementation details needed for reproducibility, including the exact BioEmu conditioning architecture, training data construction, time-lag selection, and whether BioEmu pretraining data overlaps with or is biased toward the evaluated proteins. The reproducibility statement also appears incomplete.

The scope is still narrow: three small fast-folding proteins, all from DESRES, do not fully establish generality to larger proteins, ligand-binding transitions, or systems where BioEmu priors may be less reliable.
